terminal_bridge: Kaashoek modularity thesis: dependability is not an internal property of individual stochastic components, but an invariant synthesized by the boundary structures of the supervisor. When the runtime treats foundation models strictly as unprivileged computational engines, system safety, liveness, and fairness become solvable systems engineering problems. The host supervisor governs the physical and virtual boundaries—holding candidate actions in escrow, enforcing preemption and scheduling fairness, and bounding operational expenditure—thereby allowing complex, non-deterministic agents to participate reliably in multi-tenant, mission-critical computing environments. ::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From Process Control to State Durability and Event Logs"} A supervisory control plane that maintains trajectory state exclusively within volatile host memory remains fragile in the face of inevitable machine crashes, power faults, and kernel panics. If a node fails while an agent process is suspended in an approval escrow or executing a multi-step filesystem modification, all in-memory Agent Control Blocks, tool descriptors, and pending lease tokens evaporate, leaving remote environments in partially mutated, inconsistent states. Surviving node panics and enabling retrospective auditability requires moving beyond transient process governance to durable state logging. Chapter 10 examines the mechanics of state durability: defining which trajectory events and mutated artifacts must be flushed to non-volatile storage before side effects commit, and how crash recovery protocols employ Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) to reconstruct consistent execution state from an immutable, append-only event ledger. :::
cumulative_ledger: Section 9.1 (The Supervisory Runtime): Ad-hoc loops and scripting frameworks collapse when long-horizon tasks encounter crashes, human interrupts, or budget overruns; autonomous agents require an operating system control plane that separates task logic from process governance.

Section 9.2 (The Agent Control Block): The fundamental unit of execution in an agent runtime is the trajectory process, formally tracked via an Agent Control Block (ACB) analogous to an OS Process Control Block (PCB).

Section 9.3 (Trajectory Lifecycle States): Trajectory processes transition through a formal finite state machine with strict transition guards; invalid state transitions must be rejected to prevent corrupted execution or zombie processes.

Section 9.4 (Signal Trapping Mechanisms): Agents must handle asynchronous runtime signals (`SIGINT`, `SIGPAUSE`, `SIGKILL`, `SIGBUDGET`) at clean turn boundaries without corrupting mutable state or leaving orphan child processes.

Section 9.5 (Cooperative Process Yielding): Yielding at tool boundaries and bounding model generation keep a trajectory responsive to cancellation and budgets; serving-state retention remains a separate memory-management decision.
Section 9.6 (Human Escrow Protocols): High-consequence mutations must be quarantined in cryptographic approval escrows that yield compute resources and enforce fail-safe expiration timeouts.

Section 9.7 (Single-Node Runtime Scheduling): Single-node agent runtimes must arbitrate CPU cores, host memory, sandbox pools, and inference queue slots across concurrent trajectories using fair-share scheduling algorithms.

Section 9.8 (Deterministic Resource Accounting): The supervisor must enforce hard multi-dimensional resource ceilings (steps, tokens, wall-clock time, financial cost) with progressive warning thresholds to prevent runaway billing and unconstrained infinite loops.
